description: Hydro is built by a team of mechanical engineering and architecture students from Iloilo, Philippines. We are developing an interactive map of Jezero Crater to help future Mars explorers plan fieldwork and investigate how ancient water shaped the landscape. Our project brings together orbital imagery, elevation data, Perseverance rover photos, and historical weather observations to visualize scientific insights across eight key areas of the crater.
summary:
HYDRO is an interactive map for exploring Jezero Crater on Mars. It addresses the challenge of planning a future Mars walk around sites that preserve clues to the planet’s water history. Jezero’s ancient lake and river delta make it a valuable place to study, but many areas still lack close-up observations. Crews need to know where to look and what is known about the terrain between sites.

HYDRO brings NASA and ESA imagery, elevation data, Perseverance observations, and documented terrain cautions into one map. Users can compare destinations, measure straight-line distances, review historical rover tracks, mark a potential rest stop or base camp and even record their own discoveries. Walking access and travel time are marked Unknown where evidence is insufficient, helping crews identify what they would need to verify before setting out.
details:
Why we chose Jezero

Jezero Crater preserves the remains of an ancient lake, river channels, and a delta. These features make it a valuable place to study how water moved across Mars and what its ancient environments were like. NASA’s Perseverance rover has also examined rocks and sediments closely at selected sites. We chose Jezero because users can follow a single scientific question across two scales, from the shape of the crater seen from orbit to the rocks photographed by the rover on the ground.

How to use HYDRO

HYDRO opens on an interactive Mars globe. Users can rotate the planet and select Enter Jezero to zoom directly to the study area. From there, they can search or select one of ten main areas, including Bright Angel, Kodiak, the Margin Unit, and Dacono Crater. Hawksbill Gap also has five searchable outcrops grouped under its main card.

  • Explore a place. Open a science card to see why the site matters, view credited imagery, and review available mineral evidence, historical observations, and terrain cautions. Verified rover look-around views are available at Skinner Ridge, Bright Angel, and Turquoise Bay within the Margin Unit.
  • Compare map layers. Switch between optical imagery, elevation, hillshade, and historical day and night infrared imagery. Turn on 50-meter contours to see how the crater floor, rim, and surrounding terrain change in elevation. Dated rover weather readings appear on supported cards.
  • Compare destinations. Select a starting point and destination in Directions, with optional intermediate stops. HYDRO draws a dashed line and displays the calculated straight-line distance between markers. Where archived rover tracks are available, users can inspect the recorded traverse and its estimated length. Area precaution ratings summarize sourced terrain concerns where assessed.
  • Mark a stop. Drop a temporary Landmark for a hypothetical rest stop or base camp, check its remaining distance to a destination, or use it as a new point in Directions.
  • Record an observation. In Astronaut Findings, users can enter notes about terrain, obstacles, environmental conditions, or science, then save and reopen them in the same browser. The record remains labeled User-reported · Unverified.

Who benefits and what impact we intend

HYDRO gives students and educators an interactive way to connect Jezero’s ancient water history with the landscape visible today. It also gives researchers and people exploring future mission concepts a starting point for comparing sites, reviewing what has already been observed, and identifying questions that need further investigation. For example, a user can follow Jezero’s delta on the orbital map, open a rover view of a nearby outcrop, and record a question about the layers they see. We want to make that progression from observation to a research question easier for people who are new to planetary data.

How we built it

We used TypeScript, React, HTML, and CSS to build the website, OpenLayers to render the map and align imagery and position data, and Vite to build the application. We used VS Code for development, Git and GitHub for version control, and Vercel to deploy the public site. The app runs in a web browser on standard consumer hardware.

We organized the map layers, place coordinates, science cards, and route evidence into structured data files. The optical overview combines color from ESA’s Mars Express HRSC with surface detail from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX. Regional elevation data supports the shaded relief and contours. NASA’s Mars Odyssey THEMIS provides historical infrared imagery, while Perseverance contributes rover imagery, archived positions, and dated MEDA weather readings at supported sites. Credits are displayed with the relevant images, layers, and records.

How we collected and verified the data

We started with publicly available NASA and ESA mission archives, then used published research to establish the scientific context for individual sites. For the map, we used NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX imagery for surface detail and ESA’s Mars Express HRSC imagery and elevation data for color and relief. We cropped the imagery to the Jezero study area, aligned the layers in a shared Mars coordinate system, and checked how they lined up with known landmarks. We used the elevation data to produce hillshade and 50-meter contours.

For each location, we checked published coordinates, rover position records, and image captions to establish what the evidence covered. We labeled representative map points and regional photos so users could tell when an image or marker described the surrounding area. We also checked whether archived Perseverance positions supported a historical traverse between selected sites and used dated MEDA records for weather observations where available.

We kept source links and credits with the layers, photos, and observations they support. Where the available evidence could not establish a local condition, such as footing, walking access, or travel time, we marked it Unknown. That helps users see what has already been documented and what future fieldwork could investigate.

What makes HYDRO creative

We designed HYDRO around the astronaut’s experience on the Martian surface. An explorer can review the terrain before moving, mark a rest stop or base camp, and record what they encounter along the way. Our goal is to support more efficient fieldwork and better-informed safety decisions by making terrain cautions, distance estimates, and gaps in the evidence easy to see.

Jezero has been studied from orbit and along Perseverance’s traverse, but many places still lack close-up observations. That is why we built Astronaut Findings as a field logbook. An explorer can document an unexpected obstacle, a change in footing, or a rock formation worth investigating, then save and reopen the observation in the same browser. Each entry is labeled User-reported · Unverified. In a future mission workflow, reviewed observations like these could help other researchers decide where to look next and help crews prepare for later fieldwork.

What our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy and uncertainty. A straight-line distance measures separation, and an archived rover track shows where Perseverance traveled. Walking access, walking time, and safe return remain Unknown where the evidence is insufficient. Precaution ratings apply to the documented concerns at each area.
  • Data coverage and scale. Orbital images give broad context, while rover observations cover specific locations and times. Some places have a photo or regional terrain information but lack a verified panorama or local weather reading. We show the evidence available at each location and identify gaps.
  • Readability and performance. We organized science information into expandable sections, separated crowded map labels, and used small previews for navigation. Higher-resolution panorama imagery loads when a user zooms in. Interface animations are short and respect reduced-motion settings.
  • Attribution and privacy. We kept source credits with the material they support. Findings are stored in the current browser, and the temporary Landmark clears on reload.
